1:
The verse is contested at every joint. Gill offers two readings: that the tribe, or its heads, spoke with submission and humility before it fell into idolatry, and were therefore attended to and highly honoured by the other tribes, agreeably to the saying that he who humbles himself shall be exalted; or that when he spoke there was trembling, either among neighbouring nations threatened with war or among the other tribes, who heard him with great reverence. He reports Jarchi for the first, and a rabbi who applies it to the king born of that tribe.

Wesley and Clarke take the humble sense and make it a moral. Wesley reads the tribe as humbling itself before God, the kingdom flourishing in consequence, and the death as the loss of power and glory as soon as they sinned. Clarke says the same more sharply: when he was meek and humble, of a broken heart and contrite spirit, he became great in the sight of God, rising in the divine esteem in proportion as he sank in his own; and he sets the whole chapter under that rule, that the fear of God leads to prosperity but sin to ruin. But Clarke also reports the other construction, by which the speaking is the cry that split the kingdom, so that there was a trembling or commotion and then the kingdom was exalted.

Ellicott takes that second construction outright, rendering the clause that when Ephraim uttered terror he rebelled in Israel, then committed sin through Baal and died, and referring it to the revolt of the ten tribes and their consequent abandonment of the pure traditions of worship. He suggests that this idea, and that of the verse before, may have been brought into prominence by a recent antagonism aroused by war against the southern kingdom.

Calvin rejects the whole family of readings that make the trembling the terror of the people. Some say that dread was excited when the king of that tribe exhorted the people to worship the calves, so that they were astonished and without thought obeyed the humour of an impious king; and if that sense be approved, the word may also mean that the people did not immediately embrace the perverted worship but dreaded it, as men do at new things which seem to have nothing reasonable in their favour. But these expounders, in his judgment, wholly depart from the intention of the prophet. What is set forth is the twofold state of the kingdom, so that it may be manifest that the ten tribes were rejected through their own fault and had fallen from the dignity to which God had raised them; the first clause records the honours God had given that tribe. Calvin traces those honours to their source: the younger of the two sons of Joseph was preferred to the first-begotten, so that God raised up two chiefs in that house and gave the pre-eminence to the younger.

Henry reads the verse in the light of what follows, and takes the chapter as a charge of the sin that most easily beset the nation. He sets out the provision God made to prevent it: he made himself known as their God and took them for his people in a peculiar way, declaring it by word and by works and afterwards by prophets and providences; he gave them a law forbidding them to worship any other, not merely not to own and worship another but not to acquaint themselves with any, nor make the rites of the Gentiles familiar; and he gave a reason, that there is no saviour beside him, since whatever we take for our God we expect to have for our saviour. Henry adds his own note on the prohibition, that it is a happy ignorance not to know that which we ought not to meddle with.
2:
The increase in sin is what the prophet is charging. Gill dates it from two reigns, with other deities added to the calves and to Baal, since it is common with evil men and seducers to wax worse and worse. Clarke says they increased in every kind of vice, having abandoned the great Inspirer of virtue. Calvin makes the point the obstinacy rather than the fall: they had not only in one day cast aside the pure worship and entangled themselves in superstitions, but had been obstinate in their own depravity, adding one superstition after another until there was an accumulation of madness, as if they designedly wished to subvert the law. This is what usually happens unless God draws men back, he says, since as soon as they fall away they rush headlong into evil, taking greater liberty in sinning after they have turned their back on God. Calvin also presses the silver: God bestowed it that men might carry on commerce with one another and apply it to other useful purposes, so that when they make gods of it there is an astonishing stupidity in their ingratitude, since they pervert the order of nature and forget the end for which it was given.

The hardest clause is the one about those who sacrifice. Keil and Delitzsch set out the alternatives at length: the Greek version, the fathers and many of the rabbins and Christian expositors render it as those who sacrifice men, while others, following an analogy elsewhere, render it as the sacrificers among men. They argue that the words cannot stand as an independent sentence unless the participle be arbitrarily changed to a perfect, and that joining them to what follows yields no suitable thought either way, since human sacrifices were offered not to the calves but only to another god, whose worshippers did not kiss calves. Ellicott reaches the same result more briefly: the second rendering is quite consistent with Hebrew usage, while the first compels the unwarrantable supposition that human sacrifices formed part of the calf-worship. He reports also a rendering of the earlier clause, according to their pattern of idols, following a hint in the Greek.

The kissing is explained as the standard act of adoration. Clarke describes the practice in three stages: the idol was kissed; when the statue was too high or too far off, the hand was presented in token of alliance; and then that hand was brought respectfully to the mouth and kissed, which he calls the genuine act of adoration, citing Pliny and Apuleius. He also reads the clause as a test, since a man whose conversion was doubtful could be told to come openly and kiss the calves, which would show what he was. Wesley states it plainly, that all who bring their offerings to the idols are to worship and show it by kissing them. Ellicott adds that the Greek word for worship meant originally to adore by kissing.

The four similitudes are counted by three. Clarke says four things most easy to be driven about and dissipated are employed to show how they should be scattered among the nations. Gill takes the morning cloud as what soon disappears when the sun is risen, and applies the whole to the ceasing of the kingdom and the carrying away of the people. Ellicott sharpens two of the four, rendering the second as dew that early passeth away and the last as smoke from the window, meaning the lattice beneath the roof through which it vanished. Calvin draws an inference from the threat itself: since God would not otherwise have threatened to no purpose, the people were not yet so much like the dead but that some power remained in them, and this utter destruction is denounced so that they should not think they had already suffered the last punishment, or suppose they could gather new strength.
4:
The claim of long standing is the ground of the charge. Gill takes the phrase from Egypt to cover both the bringing out and the whole time since, through the wilderness and in the land, which makes the sin great ingratitude. Keil and Delitzsch draw the contrast the verse rests on, between the idolatry of the people and the uninterrupted self-attestation of God to a faithless nation: from Egypt onward they had found no other God to be a helper and Saviour. Calvin turns the same into an answer to any excuse. Had they never known sound doctrine, there would have been some colour for alleviating their fault, since they might have pleaded that they went astray according to the common practice of men; but having been taught from infancy, and brought up as it were in the bosom of God, what excuse remains? He hears in the word thy a glance at all their fictitious gods: God is their God by his own right, being of himself and the Creator of the world, whereas the rest have their divinity only from the madness of men.

Clarke and Ellicott both report a long addition found in the Greek and not in the Hebrew, in which God declares himself the maker of the heavens and the earth and says he did not show them that they should walk after them. Clarke suggests it might once have been in the Hebrew text; Ellicott reports that Jerome could not find it in any Hebrew copy of his day and pronounced it spurious. Wesley draws the inference from the commandment, that having been forbidden to know any other God they should in gratitude have known no other.

Knowing in the wilderness is read as adoption. Keil and Delitzsch say the verb, when used of God, is an attestation of his love and care, so that to have known them in the desert means to have adopted them in love; they gloss the rare word for the land as the burning heat in which men famish with thirst. Gill lists what the knowing amounted to: feeding with manna and quails, guiding in the way, and protecting from enemies where there was neither food nor drink but scorpions and beasts of prey. Henry calls such help at an exigency a peculiar obligation never to be forgotten, since the God who fed them there was a friend at need, able to victual so vast an army where, if miracles had not been their daily bread, all must have perished. Calvin turns the word into a doctrine of two knowledges, and cites the correction Paul makes to the Galatians, after ye have known God, or rather after ye are known by him; since God anticipates men by his gratuitous goodness, ingratitude is shameful because they do not seek to know him in return.

The pasture is where the gift becomes the danger. Gill compares a flock brought from short commons into good pasture, filling itself to the full and indulging to excess. Henry says God gave both plenty and dainties and they did not spare it, and that it would have promised better if they had been more moderate and had learned to deny themselves; but they were filled, and their heart was exalted, their luxury making them proud and secure. Clarke states the rule that follows, that he who exalteth himself shall be abased. Ellicott renders the phrase as they pastured, and sums it in one line: the gifts of divine love concealing the giver. Keil and Delitzsch note that the reproof is taken almost word for word from a warning in the law, so that the very thing Moses warned of has happened. Calvin makes it proof of an intractable nature, since after being fed when hungry in the desert they rejected God in their fulness and, like ferocious horses, kicked against him.
7:
The three beasts are read as a change of character in God. Calvin says the prophet adopts these similitudes because the people were torpid through their own flatteries, and self-confidence so inebriates hypocrites that they despise all threatenings. God is in his own nature merciful and kind, and when he says he will be like a lion he puts on as it were another character, which is done on account of the wickedness of men, according to the saying that with the gentle he will be gentle and with the perverse perverse. Calvin is careful to add that perversity does not properly belong to God, the similitude being borrowed from men so that they may not continue to flatter themselves when he is displeased with them.

Each beast is identified as closely as the commentators can manage. Gill notes that the word used signifies an old lion, which though slower in pursuit is more cruel when it has got its prey. Clarke takes the first for the black lion frequent in Ethiopia, and the second for a beast named from its spotted skin, since to be spotted is the signification of the root; he describes its manner, hiding in thick bushwood near where prey is expected and springing suddenly upon it, which is the allusion in the clause about observing them by the way, so that they should be greatly harassed even on the road into captivity. Keil and Delitzsch derive the same verb from a root meaning to look round, and so to lie in wait. Ellicott corrects the tense, since the verb is not future but have become, and reports a textual difference: the received reading follows the Targum, while the Greek, Latin and Syriac versions rest on a slightly different reading found in some manuscripts, which they render as a panther on the way to Assyria.

The bear and the tearing are described with equal care. Gill says the creature is fierce at any time but especially when bereaved, being fond of its whelps and having taken pains to lick them into form, so that it falls with the utmost fury on man or beast it meets. Clarke calls it a figure for excessive ferocity, and explains the next clause by the habits of beasts of prey, which go first to the seat of the blood, delighting in that more than in the most delicate flesh; the old strong lion drinks the blood, tears the flesh and breaks the bones for the marrow, and the beast that follows he takes for the animal which hunts down prey and then stands by to pick the bones, having been called for that reason the provider and the waiting-man of the lion.

What the enclosure of the heart means divides two. Ellicott says it is the covering of the heart, not the pericardium but the breast in which the claws of the beast are fastened. Calvin rejects as over-refined those who take it for obstinate hardness, granting that the prophets sometimes call a heart hard, or covered with fatness, when it is not pliant, but holding that the allusion here is to the savageness of the bear, since it is the most cruel kind of death when the beast aims with claws and teeth at the heart itself and tears the bowels of a man. He allows that the prophet may still glance at the hardness of the people while keeping his similitude, and notes that the last clause drops the figure altogether, since God means that all the wild beasts would be his ministers to execute his judgment. Calvin draws the use: if we are by nature slothful and careless, and indulge our own delusions unless stirred up, such figurative representations are what shake off our tardiness and show how dreadful the judgment of God is.
9:
The blame is laid where it belongs, and all agree on that much. Gill says that though God was a lion and a leopard and a bear to them, their destruction was not owing to him but to themselves, their own sins bringing it on and provoking the wrath already expressed; the clause is put in to clear God of any imputation and to lay the fault where it should be. Clarke says the same, that these evils came not by immediate infliction but as the consequences of their own crimes, the terrifying figures showing only what they would meet from the hand of the Assyrians, God being represented as doing what he only permits to be done. Henry makes the verse the summary of all that follows, and states the rule sharply: wilful sinners are self-destroyers, and obstinate impenitence is the grossest self-murder, so that those destroyed of the destroyer have their blood upon their own head.

What the subject of the verb is remains open. Gill offers three: the calf and the worship of it, as one interpreter has it; or their king, taken by anticipation from the next verse; or, as he prefers, all the sins already named. He reports a fourth from a scholar who takes the word in the sense of burning, so that by their sins they had made an enemy of him who is a consuming fire, and in whom otherwise they would have had help. Calvin weighs the grammar. Some supply the calf, which he calls strained; others suppose a change of person, which he is inclined to adopt, since that mode of speaking is common, so that the sense would be that Israel has destroyed himself. But on fuller weighing he prefers to take it indefinitely: something has destroyed thee, as though God said, inquire now who has destroyed thee. On that reading God names no author of the ruin, but shows that its cause is to be sought in some other than himself.

The second clause is the harder half. Henry offers two senses and keeps both. It might have been: God would have helped and healed them, but they would not be helped, being resolutely set on their own destruction, which aggravates the condemnation of sinners, since they not only did what tended to their own ruin but opposed the offers made to prevent it. Or it may be: their case is bad but not desperate, and the words are an invitation to come and be helped. Henry calls this a plank thrown out after shipwreck, magnifying not only the power of God, who can help when things are at the worst, but the riches of his grace, that he will help those who have destroyed themselves.

Clarke and Ellicott both report attempts to alter the sense. Clarke gives the received rendering, that though they have destroyed themselves their help is found in God alone, and notes that others read the clause as a question, who will help thee, on a change of one letter; he observes that although the Syriac countenances this, no manuscript yet collated supports it, and he does not think it the true reading. Ellicott takes the opposite view, holding the close of the verse rhetorically abrupt in a way the English version misses, and rendering it that their help is against God, with the words thou hast rebelled to be supplied; he closes with a saying of another writer, that their captivity is from themselves and their redemption from God. Calvin reads the verse as saying more than that they had rejected what was offered: they were past hope, and there was a hidden cause preventing God from bringing them aid in their extreme necessity, since if the wickedness and ingratitude of the people had not hindered, he would have continued to show them favour.
10:
The opening clause is read as a promise or as a taunt. Gill gives both: God will be their king, governor, protector and defender, confirming that their help is in him; or else, with the Targum and others, where is thy king now, that he may save thee in all thy cities, the question asked ironically of the king they had demanded in rejecting God, who was now either dead or taken by the enemy or unable to help. Ellicott takes only the second, rendering it where, pray, is thy king, that he may save thee. Wesley keeps both and makes them a sequence: God would have been their king to govern and save, but they refused him in both, and now he will be their king to punish. Calvin makes the first clause a statement of unchanging character, since no overshadowing happens to God; if the Israelites complain that he no longer pursues his usual course of kindness the complaint is most false, and when they cry and are not answered the way to his favour must have been closed by their own wickedness.

Which king was given in anger divides them sharply. Gill rejects the Assyrian king, since the second clause cannot be said of him, and rejects the first king of the ten tribes, who was given in anger not to them; he prefers the first king of the whole nation, given at the request of the people though in anger, since by asking they rejected God as their king. Clarke names the same king and finds the taking away in the defeat before the Philistines, but reports others who make the king given the Assyrian conqueror and the king taken away the last of the northern line. Calvin takes the founder of the northern kingdom instead, and draws a lesson from the beginning: it was a cursed beginning and would be a cursed end, since the election was not lawful but came of an impious wilfulness by which the people revolted from the family of David, and nothing successful could proceed from so inauspicious a beginning. Ellicott corrects the tenses to present, giving and taking away, and applies the words to the whole succession of kings taken away generation after generation, some by violent death, ending with the last of them. Clarke adds that the demand was made when they cast off the divine government.

The binding up of the iniquity is agreed to be a delay, not a pardon. Gill takes it generally of all their sins, bound up and not loosed, not remitted because they were impenitent, kept as in a bag or purse to be opened in proper time in open court, or laid up among the treasures of divine omniscience. Clarke says it is registered in a court of justice, the death warrant in store and to be produced in due time, so that though the judgment is not presently inflicted it will surely come. Wesley makes the binding the charging of sins upon the sinner, as loosing is forgiving, and says the hiding is not from God but a laying up with him against the day of recompense. Keil and Delitzsch note that the phrase applies a verse of the law, the first word meaning bound in a bundle like something one wishes to keep with great care, and the second carefully preserved so as not to be lost. Calvin adds the sting: hypocrites flatter themselves in vain while vengeance is suspended, since God may connive for a time but does not sleep; writings may perish when they are spread abroad, but what is laid up under a seal always remains, so that it would be far better to suffer immediate punishment, since then the memory of the sin would pass away. Ellicott says the hiding away for ultimate disclosure prepares us for the terrible words that follow.
13:
The travailing woman is read as suddenness and then as delay. Gill takes the sorrows for afflictions and calamities, denoting their suddenness and inevitableness. Clarke describes the critical time in a birth when the mother may be eased by skilful help but which, if neglected, endangers both lives, and applies it to the time when the people might have returned to God and would not. Wesley makes it a child that sticks in the birth, one while willing and another while unwilling to return, and dying under the delay. Ellicott notices the shift, that the people are first addressed as the travailing woman but the imagery then passes to the unborn child which tarries just where it should issue into the light of the world. Calvin holds that the words mean the opposite of what some interpreters make them: they take it that the people will not stay in the breaking forth, whereas the prophet means that they would stop there, which they would not do if they had a sound mind.

The next verse is the crux of the chapter, and it divides the commentators into two parties. Keil and Delitzsch state it flatly: the verse contains a promise and not a threat, and that fact would hardly have been overlooked by so many commentators had they not been led, out of regard to the verses on either side, to put force upon the words, taking the first clauses either as questions, should I redeem, or as conditional, I would redeem. Calvin is one of those they name. He argues that God does not here simply promise salvation but shows himself ready to save while the wickedness of the people stands in the way, so that the promise is conditional, and that those are mistaken who take the words as the usual mitigation added after reproof. He allows that some render the clauses in the subjunctive and says they faithfully set forth the design of the prophet, though the future tense may be kept.

Ellicott lays both parties out. The rendering should be, where is thy plague and where thy sting, as the Greek has it and as it is quoted in one of the epistles, though the received rendering is supported by other versions and by many modern expositors. Many Christian interpreters take the verse as the sudden outburst of a gracious promise, and read the last clause to mean that the gift and calling of God are without repentance. The objection Ellicott raises is that in the same breath the prophet rushes on to the most sweeping condemnation; and he reports others who accordingly read the whole as questions expecting no, with a summons to death and the grave to strike. He observes that the apostle called upon them in derisive irony to do their very worst at the moment they were about to be cast into the lake of fire.

Clarke and Wesley take the promise without hesitation and carry it furthest. Clarke reads the captivity as a grave in which the people lie dead and buried, like the vision of the valley of dry bones, and says the gracious purpose of God shall not be utterly defeated; he hears the prophet exclaim in the person of the Redeemer, who brings into the reign of death the principle of its destruction, the Prince of life lying for a time under that power to destroy it. He distinguishes the two words, one the state of the dead, which must deliver up all its dead, the other the principle of corruption, which shall be annihilated because the body shall be raised incorruptible. Wesley makes the ransom both by price and by power, restricts it to those that repent and believe, and calls it a glorious promise interposed in the midst of all these judgments.
15:
The opening clause is a play on the name, and the voices differ on whose fruitfulness is meant. Clarke notes the wordplay, since the verb comes from the same root as the name of the tribe. Gill sets aside the reading that takes the words of the Redeemer, who would increase his brethren and be as noxious to death as the east wind is to growing things, and refers them instead to the tribe, either to a spiritual fruitfulness in the last days when the people return and bring forth the fruit of good works, or to what follows. Calvin refers the fruitfulness to the ancient blessing, when the younger of two brothers was preferred in honour to the firstborn, a prophecy really fulfilled, since that tribe excelled all the rest but one in number and in other respects. What Calvin reproves is the ingratitude: they ought to have ascribed the eminence to the gratuitous goodness of God, and instead became inflated with pride, abusing their wealth to foster it, since their audacity in rebellion came precisely from having increased among their brethren.

Keil and Delitzsch read the same clause as a reason rather than a concession. Following one commentator they take the verse to prove that the promised grace of redemption would certainly stand firm, and argue on grammatical grounds that the particle can be neither temporal nor conditional, since neither yields a suitable thought, the tribe being neither fruitful then nor likely to become so; a hypothetical rendering, should he be a fruitful child, cannot be sustained, since the particle used is confined to cases where a circumstance is assumed to be real.

The east wind is identified without dispute. Clarke says that as the east wind parches and blasts all vegetation, so the conqueror shall blast and destroy the state. Wesley calls the enemy as pernicious to their estate as that wind is to fruits, explains the phrase about the wind of the Lord as the usual Hebrew superlative for a mighty enemy, and notes that the winds from the south-east were of all the most hot and blasting. Calvin hears in the drying of the spring and fountain a declaration that it lay in the power of God to take away what he had given.

The last verse is disputed only in where it belongs. Gill notes that the following chapter begins here in the Hebrew copies and in the Targum and many versions, but thinks it better to conclude the present chapter, since the verse explains the figurative expressions used just before. Calvin says the same, that the verse has been improperly separated from the former chapter, since the prophet enters on no new subject but confirms what he had said of the ultimate destruction. Gill identifies the city as the metropolis of the ten tribes, whose desolation was accomplished by the Assyrian king signified by the east wind, and takes the head city as standing for the whole land laid waste at the same time. Clarke says the rest is a simple prophetic declaration of the cruelties to be exercised on a hapless people. Keil and Delitzsch render the first verb as to atone, that is, to bear the guilt or the punishment, and note that as a matter of fact the expiation consisted in the conquest and devastation of the city; they observe an anomaly in the construction of the last clause, which they explain from the rarity of certain feminine forms. Calvin sets out the three things the verse contains: that it was all over with the city and the kingdom, since God could by no means bring them to repentance; that he would do this justly, because he had been provoked, so that they suffered only the punishment they deserved; and what kind their punishment would be, lest they should think the enemy came by chance.
